pests.name: Onion thrips
pests.identification_seasoned: Tiny slender insects that rasp silvery streaks and flecks into the leaf folds; heavy feeding stunts the tops and can spread disease.
pests.identification_beginner: Very small insects that leave silvery streaks and specks on the leaves, often in the crease where leaves meet. Heavy feeding stunts the plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) build through warm, dry spells, sheltering in the leaf axils where sprays miss them.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny insect called onion thrips. It multiplies fast in warm, dry weather and hides in the tight folds of the leaves.
pests.management_seasoned: Keep plants vigorous and watered, hose off light infestations, and rotate away from alliums; treat persistent outbreaks per local extension guidance.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the plants healthy and watered, spray them off with water if thrips are light, and do not plant alliums in the same spot every year. For heavy infestations, ask your local extension office what to use.

pests.name: Onion maggot
pests.identification_seasoned: Wilting, yellowing seedlings and rotting shanks riddled by small white larvae; stand loss is worst in cool, wet springs.
pests.identification_beginner: Young plants wilt and yellow, and the white bottoms rot with small white grubs inside. Worst in cool, wet spring weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the onion maggot fly (Delia antiqua), whose eggs are laid at the plant base; populations carry over in allium residue.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae (maggots) of a small fly that lays eggs at the base of the plants. They survive in leftover onion debris.
pests.management_seasoned: Rotate away from alliums, remove crop residue, and use floating row cover at emergence to block egg-laying.
pests.management_beginner: Do not plant alliums in the same place each year, clean up old onion scraps, and cover young plants with row-cover fabric so the fly cannot lay eggs on them.

pests.name: Allium leafminer
pests.identification_seasoned: Rows of white dots punched down the leaf where adults feed, then larvae mining inside the leaves and shank, leaving distorted, scarred tops.
pests.identification_beginner: Lines of small white dots on the leaves, then little grubs tunneling inside, leaving twisted, scarred leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: The allium leafminer (Phytomyza gymnostoma), active in spring and fall, lays eggs in the leaves; larvae mine down toward the base.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly whose grubs tunnel inside allium leaves. It is active in spring and fall.
pests.management_seasoned: Cover plants with insect netting during the spring and fall flights, rotate away from alliums, and remove infested debris.
pests.management_beginner: Cover the plants with fine netting in spring and fall when the fly is active, rotate where you plant alliums, and clear away infested leaves.

diseases.name: Botrytis neck rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: A soft, sunken rot at the neck and leaf bases, often with gray mold; favored by lingering leaf wetness and crowding.
diseases.identification_beginner: Soft, rotten spots at the base of the leaves, sometimes with gray mold. It is worse when the tops stay wet and the plants are crowded.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis infection of wet, crowded foliage; overhead watering and excess nitrogen worsen it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold that gets into wet, crowded leaves. Watering over the top and too much fertilizer make it worse.
diseases.management_seasoned: Water at the base, space for airflow, avoid excess nitrogen, and harvest on dry days.
diseases.management_beginner: Water at the base, do not crowd the plants, go easy on fertilizer, and harvest when the leaves are dry.

diseases.name: Fusarium basal rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: Browning and decay at the basal plate with roots dying back; plants yellow, wilt, and pull up easily.
diseases.identification_beginner: The very bottom of the plant turns brown and rots and the roots die, so the plant yellows and pulls up easily.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Fusarium that persists for years and is favored by warm soil; wounds and maggot damage open the door.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that stays in the ground for years and likes warm soil. Injuries and insect damage let it in.
diseases.management_seasoned: Rotate out of alliums for several years, choose resistant stock where available, and avoid wounding the plants.
diseases.management_beginner: Do not grow alliums in the same spot for several years, pick resistant varieties if you can, and handle the plants gently.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting plants with a fluffy white fungal mat and small black sclerotia at the base; the root system rots away.
diseases.identification_beginner: Plants turn yellow and wilt, and you find a fluffy white mold with tiny black specks at the base. The roots rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The soilborne fungus Sclerotium cepivorum, whose sclerotia survive in soil for many years; cool, moist conditions favor it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus whose tough resting bodies survive in the ground for many years. Cool, damp conditions make it worse.
diseases.management_seasoned: There is no cure once soil is infested; use clean transplants, never move infested soil, and rotate alliums far away for many years.
diseases.management_beginner: Once the soil has it, there is no cure, so start with clean plants, avoid moving infested soil, and keep alliums far from that spot for many years.
